summary.text: De Moivre's formula connects complex numbers and trigonometry, using the expression cos x + i sin x, sometimes abbreviated cis x.
Expanding one side and comparing real and imaginary parts gives expressions for cos nx and sin nx in terms of cos x and sin x.
As written it is not valid for non-integer powers, but generalizations of it give explicit expressions for the nth roots of unity.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: Abraham de Moivre, who never stated it in his works

facts.label: Valid powers
facts.value: Whole-number powers, even when x is a complex number

facts.label: Proof method
facts.value: Mathematical induction covers the natural numbers

facts.label: Chebyshev link
facts.value: The cos nx formula is a Chebyshev polynomial of cos x

paragraphs.heading: What the formula says
paragraphs.text: De Moivre's formula, also called de Moivre's theorem or de Moivre's identity, says that for any real number x and any integer n, raising cos x + i sin x to the power n gives cos n x + i sin n x. Here i is the imaginary unit, the number whose square is −1, so i² = −1. The bracketed expression cos x + i sin x is sometimes shortened to cis x.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is useful
paragraphs.text: The formula is a bridge between complex numbers and trigonometry. Take x to be real, expand the left side, and then match real parts with real parts and imaginary parts with imaginary parts. That gives expressions for cos nx and sin nx built only from cos x and sin x. The expression for cos nx turns out to be the Chebyshev polynomial Tₙ evaluated at cos x.

paragraphs.heading: A name and a successor
paragraphs.text: The formula carries the name of Abraham de Moivre, yet he never stated it in any of his works. It came before Euler's formula, in which x is measured in radians rather than degrees: eⁱˣ = cos x + i sin x. Euler's formula sets out the basic link between the trigonometric functions and the complex exponential function.

paragraphs.heading: Proving it step by step
paragraphs.text: One proof uses mathematical induction. The case n = 0 holds plainly, because cos(0x) + i sin(0x) = 1 + 0i = 1. Next one shows that if the statement is true for some k, it is also true for k + 1, so it holds for every natural number. Negative powers are handled separately by looking at an exponent of −n for natural n, and together these cover all integers.

paragraphs.heading: Where it stops working
paragraphs.text: As written, the formula fails for powers that are not integers. Raising a complex number to a non-integer power gives several possible answers rather than one. On the other hand, x need not be real: with the usual extension of sine and cosine to complex inputs, the formula still holds for any complex x.

paragraphs.heading: Finding roots
paragraphs.text: A modest extension of the formula finds the n-th roots of a complex number, for any non-zero integer n. Write z in polar form, z = r (cos x + i sin x). Its n-th roots are then r^(1/n) [cos((x + 2πk)/n) + i sin((x + 2πk)/n)], as k runs through the integers from 0 to |n| − 1. This version is sometimes also called de Moivre's formula. Generalizations like this give explicit expressions for the nth roots of unity, the complex numbers z with zⁿ = 1.
